summary: At the Moon's south pole the Sun and Earth hover only a few degrees above the horizon, so a single ridge can decide whether a lander has power, a link home, both, or neither. Existing tools for checking this are hard to use. Lunar Landing Site Navigator turns the question into three clicks: what do you want to build (11 categories, 31 project types, or a custom one), when (2026–2040), and what kind of mission (autonomous, short crewed, long crewed or permanent base). The app ranks all 13 NASA candidate landing regions with a plain-language explanation, then opens any of them as an interactive 3D terrain built from lunar laser altimetry. Sun and Earth are placed hour by hour from ephemerides, with a 360° horizon panorama and a timeline of light and communication. Users can then place their own modules on the terrain and watch their shadows move through the lunar day. It makes illumination and Earth visibility readable in seconds for mission planners, educators and the public, and it moves the question from "where can we land?" to "where can we stay?".
details:
What it does. Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web app that answers one question for the lunar south pole: which of the 13 candidate regions is best for my project, in my time window, on my kind of mission?

The user picks (1) a project type from 11 categories and 31 sub-types or a custom type with five importance sliders (Sun, Earth, short night, flat terrain, ice); (2) a period: 2026–2028, 2028–2030, 2030–2036 or 2036–2040; (3) a mission category: autonomous, short crewed (best 7-day window with Sun and Earth together), or long crewed / permanent base (shortest nights over the whole period). The app ranks the 13 regions on a map of the pole and explains each score. A click opens a region with four key numbers (Sun, Earth, both together, longest night), a 360° horizon panorama with the Sun and Earth paths, a timeline coloured by state (Sun + Earth / Sun only / Earth only / neither), and a 3D terrain tile with a time slider.
Beyond the brief. The challenge asks for fast comparison of Sun and Earth against the local horizon. We added the step that follows: designing on the site. Users place their own box-shaped modules on the 3D terrain (width, length, height, rotation). Each module stands upright, rests on the highest terrain point under its footprint, gets a foundation down to the ground, casts a shadow that follows the Sun hour by hour, and is checked against rules: outside the region, overlap, minimum spacing, slope, foundation height. Layouts are saved per region and can be copied and pasted.
How it works. Offline, a Python pipeline computes: Sun direction and Earth position in the Moon-fixed frame (SPICE, DE440) every hour from 2026 to 2041; 360° horizons out to 250 km from LOLA elevation data (40 m/px) for 676 measurement points (52 per region); illumination maps; and 512×512 terrain tiles. The result is static data files. In the browser, a JavaScript engine reads them, scores regions, and renders the terrain in Three.js. There is no backend, no account and no install; it works on a phone.
What we found with it. Connecting Ridge has the best energy conditions (Sun up to 85% of the time, longest night 146 h). Malapert Massif has the best communication (31% of its area sees Earth at least 90% of the time; Sun and Earth together up to 62%). Good spots are tiny: in no region do points with at least 70% Sun cover more than 0.1% of the area, so choosing the spot inside a region matters as much as choosing the region. Only Connecting Ridge stays inside the 192 h darkness limit of an uncrewed rover, and no point at 2 m height meets the 36 h limit of a crewed rover, which means crewed bases need energy storage or a reactor. The tool makes this visible in seconds.
Benefits and intended impact. Mission planners get a fast first screening and a shared picture for discussion. Educators and the public get an intuitive way to see why the poles are hard and why every ridge counts. Early-stage teams can test a base layout before any detailed engineering.
Tools. Python (NumPy, SPICE), Node.js for tests and build, JavaScript (ES modules), Three.js 0.180, HTML/CSS, Space Grotesk font, Blender (reference scene of Mons Mouton used for cross-checking). Hosted as a static page.
Validation. Ephemerides agree with JPL Horizons to 0.001° and with our Blender reference scene to about 0.01°. Shadow lengths on flat ground match h / tan(elevation) within 0.04%. Module-to-terrain contact was checked against dense sampling on 78 modules on slopes of 15° or more (largest difference 0.0006 m). Illumination at Connecting Ridge (86%) is a lower bound compared with the published 92.1% (Gläser et al., 2018), because 40 m terrain flattens narrow ridges; the app says so.
Creativity. We turned a visualization challenge into a decision-and-design tool, kept the interface to black background, white text and one question per screen, and deliberately show no agency or mission names, so the tool stays neutral and works for any actor.
Factors we considered. Honest uncertainty (lower bounds, 40 m terrain, shadows only from terrain inside the tile), assumptions marked as assumptions (example module sizes and thresholds are not real hardware), accessibility (status shown with symbol and text, not colour alone), performance on phones (smaller meshes and shadow maps), and scope (13 candidate regions of the 2022 list, static data, no backend).
